entry.title: How to Flip a Video With FFmpeg (hflip and vflip Are Mirrors, Not Rotates, and -c copy Cannot Do Them)
entry.summary:
Short answer: to flip a video with FFmpeg, re-encode through hflip or vflip: ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vf hflip -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a copy flipped.mp4
hflip is a left–right mirror. vflip is a top–bottom mirror. The frame size stays the same (here, 720×1280). That is not a rotate: transpose=1 would turn this clip into 1280×720. And despite what autocomplete offers for "ffmpeg flip video without re encoding", a flip is a video filter, so -c:v copy is rejected: Filtering and streamcopy cannot be used together. Audio can still be stream-copied. Below are pixel-exact measurements on a real 8-second clip, a small Python module, and five pytest checks.

entry.title: Deciding what to cut in a talking-head video: pauses are easy, retakes are not
entry.summary: I'm building Cutora, an editor that makes the first cut of a talking-head video. Most of the interesting problems turned out not to be "AI" problems at all. They're timing problems. Here's how the cut is decided, and where it still goes wrong. Everything starts from a transcript where every word has a start and end time. The cut is planned on words, then rendered on media. If the word times are wrong, every later rule inherits the error, so most of our bugs live here, not in the "smart" parts. Long pauses get cut, with a short beat left around the words so speech doesn't sound stapled together. Short pauses stay, because they're how people breathe. We don't expose a millisecond threshold; creators pick a pacing and can restore any single cut on the timeline. The trap: a loudness threshold …
